paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Hill took place at Hartwell, Hart County, Georgia, in early March 1881, when a crowd of about three hundred people gathered around the jail threatening to lynch Hill, a Black prisoner recaptured after the killing of the county jailer. No attack on the jail was reported, and Hill was later tried, convicted and hanged under a court sentence before a crowd of several thousand.

Hill, also known as Henry Turner, had been held in the Hartwell jail for some months on a burglary charge and had tried to escape the previous November by burning the jail, according to the Hartwell Sun. Just after sunset on 23 February 1881, jailer Thomas V. Skelton went into the jail to feed him and was found dead in the hall that night with his head crushed, and Hill was gone. An Atlanta dispatch said Hill had worked loose the bolt of the food trap in his cell door, crawled through it, and struck Skelton with a piece of plank from his bunk.

The next morning a coroner's jury returned a verdict that Skelton had been murdered by Hill and recommended that the Governor offer a $500 reward. A News and Courier brief from Anderson said the fugitive was thought to have crossed into South Carolina and described him as very tall, pock-marked and with a double thumb.

A short wire item reported that Hill had been caught in the woods while roasting a potato at a fire. In the fuller version of the item, "at last advices" three hundred people were hovering around the jail threatening to lynch him. The item gives no date or place of the capture beyond the woods, and no later report describes what the crowd did or how it dispersed.

Hill was tried and convicted of murder in late March and sentenced to hang on 22 April, which the Anderson Intelligencer understood would be the first capital sentence carried out in Hart County. According to a dispatch to the Atlanta Constitution, he was hanged on that day under a guard of two hundred armed men commanded by J. G. McCurry, with the bar-rooms closed and "no confusion and but little excitement." On the gallows Hill admitted the killing and blamed cards and whiskey, and a correspondent of the Keowee Courier described him warning his children against both.

The threat itself reached print only as one line in the "Crime" columns of a Wisconsin and a Missouri weekly on 10 March, where Hill was called "the butcher" and the crowd was mentioned without comment. A Missouri paper had run the capture sentence alone five days earlier, and the Chillicothe Crisis printed a separate item placing the killing at "Hartwell, Ark."

Papers in upstate South Carolina, near Hartwell, followed the case most closely, and the Anderson Intelligencer reprinted the Hartwell Sun's long account of the killing. That account mourned Skelton as "one of our best citizens" and called Hill a "notoriously desperate character" and "the infuriated negro," while a Mississippi paper described him as "a big black negro." The hanging was carried by wire as far as Memphis, Wheeling and Sacramento, each giving eight thousand spectators.

The hanging is dated Friday, 22 April by the local dispatch and the Keowee correspondent, but 23 April or "Saturday" in wire versions. Most reports put the crowd at the hanging at eight thousand, but the Keowee correspondent, noting that an ex-sheriff supposed 8,000, thought there were not more than 5,000.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Hill
bases: A wire brief reported a crowd of three hundred around the Hartwell jail threatening to lynch Henry Hill after his capture (A6, A7); no attack on the jail is reported, and Hill was later tried and legally hanged (A9, A15).

A crowd of three hundred threatened to lynch Hill for the jailer's killing (A6, A7), but no one was killed by it; Hill was hanged after a trial and conviction under a court sentence (A9, A15, A16), which is a legal execution, so this is a threatened lynching only.

The crowd and threat appear only in one wire brief carried word for word by two papers on the same day (A6, A7); the earliest copy of the item mentions only the capture (A5), and no later report of the trial or hanging mentions a crowd at the jail (A9, A15, A16).

framing.detail: Northern and Midwestern weeklies ran the capture-and-threat item as one line in a 'Crime' column, calling Hill 'the butcher' without comment on the threatened lynching.
The Hartwell Sun account reprinted in Anderson praised Skelton as 'one of our best citizens' and described Hill as a 'notoriously desperate character' and 'the infuriated negro'.
Upstate South Carolina papers covered the trial and hanging as a lawful execution, noting it would be the first capital sentence carried out in Hart county.
